root_idea.summary: The root centers on undergoing hardship and on a condition opposed to ease, felicity, and prosperity.
root_idea.development: The semantic development connects enduring difficulty with becoming wretched or unfortunate; the reciprocal Form III develops this into struggling with another person or with a difficulty. The supplied root discussion distinguishes the hamzated root شقأ, whose meaning changes, from the شقو family.

qac_form_accounting.reason: Displayed under the normalized Form I perfect citation form شَقِيَ.
Distinct Quran-attested noun meaning wretchedness or misery.
Distinct Quran-attested elative adjective used substantively.

senses.definition: To be or become wretched, unfortunate, unhappy, or miserable.
senses.usage_conditions: Describes a state contrary to prosperity or felicity, including resulting misfortune or unhappiness.

senses.definition: To suffer hardship, distress, or fatigue.
senses.usage_conditions: Used of undergoing difficulty or strain; in the Quranic Taha constructions, it describes the suffering or distress a person would undergo. Fatigue is a narrower realization of this hardship sense.

senses.definition: Wretched, unfortunate, unhappy, or deprived of felicity; a person in such a state.
senses.usage_conditions: Used adjectivally and substantively. In the construction شَقِيًّا بِدُعَائِكَ, the sense is idiomatically extended to being disappointed or without a favorable response to one's supplication.

senses.definition: Wretchedness, misery, or a condition opposed to felicity.
senses.usage_conditions: A nominal expression for the state of being wretched; in شِقْوَتُنَا, it denotes the speakers' prevailing misery or misfortune.

senses.definition: More or most wretched, unfortunate, or miserable; the one characterized by the greatest wretchedness.
senses.usage_conditions: An elative form used substantively in Quranic contexts, with the comparison sometimes implicit in a definite or contextual description.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To struggle or contend with another, or with a difficulty, in order to prevail or overcome; to vie in endurance.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A reciprocal Form III construction used for mutual striving, contest, or endurance.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To treat someone with hardness, harshness, or ill-nature.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative or extended Form III use describing harsh treatment.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To cause someone to be wretched, unfortunate, unhappy, or in distress.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A transitive Form IV causative construction.
A separate rare lexical use, distinct from the wretchedness-related verb and adjective.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Unprosperousness, misfortune, unhappiness, or a state of distress contrary to felicity.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: This nominal is described as either otherworldly or worldly; worldly wretchedness may concern the soul, body, or external circumstances.
A narrower use than the general term for fatigue: every instance of this condition involves fatigue, but not every fatigue is شَقَاوَةٌ.
A tropical comparative or superlative use, distinct from the Quranic sense of greatest wretchedness.

lane_unit_coverage.note: Covers wretchedness, hardship, and the nominal شِقْوَة forms.
Mutual striving and surpassing are covered by the broader struggle sense.
Vying in endurance is covered by the struggle and endurance sense.
Only identifies verbal-noun or substantive status; no additional meaning.
Wretched or unfortunate adjective/substantive, including the Quranic supplication construction.
Independent شَقَاوَةٌ nominal and its classifications.
Separate comparative or superlative fatigue use.

cautions: A printed historical Quran citation associated with a reading is not converted into a modern surah:ayah location; the example for شِقْوَةٌ uses 23:106 because that location is independently supplied by QAC and the Quran-focused evidence.
The comb-related entries are kept separate from the wretchedness-related senses. The supplied root discussion itself notes that hamzation can change the meaning.
